(Moved from CSLib)

cc @Shreyas Srinivas

I read the PR description here and I'm a bit confused about how this kind of model could ever be used to reason about something like a turing machine. How can you rule out machines which skip all the 'queries' and just do all the computation in pure lean? I think this is what is described in the second point about subversion, but in the case of e.g. TMs I don't see any way around the problem. It seems to me to be a pretty fundamental limitation of a monadic approach.

I would have thought that in order to reach the level of generality you describe (where we can use the same abstractions to reason about both turing machines and abstract sorting algorithms) we would need to parameterise Prog by the allowed combinators, not just the allowed queries.

There’s a few different answers to this question(s)

  1. As I have noted in the PR description, an algorithm is part of the spec. If you write an algorithm named heapsort but internally write mergeSort, nothing lean does can save you from making errors. This doesn’t change even if you have a deeply embedded language with no monadic pure functions. You’d have an nlog⁡nn \log nnlogn algorithm that sorts correctly either way. This also applies to TMs. You always need to check your spec.
  2. you can extend the uniform correctness spec to Turing machines. In principle if the “move left” query was modelled by the TM moving right and vice versa and the TM output read from right to left (imagine I am looking at the TM through a mirror), your sneaky pure code will not pass the uniform correctness theorem. this theorem would state the correctness of a TMs function through the model. I don’t have time to write this out.
  3. Of course stating every theorem in this “uniform” shape would be tedious and severe overkill. But for proving upper bounds it is perfectly fine to expect users to read the code and check what has been written. If you want to rubber duck a TM sometimes you really don’t care about one part of it. In these cases you really just want to be allowed to use a pure function. You might ask why bother with all these query model stuff ; I’d say it still lets you define a model and speak of reductions.

Also note that Prog being FreeM is a design choice to keep formalization lightweight for theory’s sake. My initial attempt was a deep embedding. A nice thing about the idea is, you could always write a deeply embedded version of Prog. Then you could prove TM algorithms in this version to be extensionally equal to a FreeM variant if you want to be certain of its correctness and complexity. You would have already proved all the correctness and complexity properties for this FreeM version.

as I recently discussed with @Samuel Schlesinger you could also flip this direction.
TL DR: this is a design tradeoff. The design can be extended to a deeply embedded DSL for models like TMs

I personally prefer working with explicit models like Turing machines and circuits, but I understand why some people might want a more ergonomic but somehow "leakier" model. Especially if you're doing everything by hand, it is a reasonable tradeoff. When you are making more complex proofs and definitions with AI assistance, the tradeoffs seem to favor explicit models in any case because then you can trust the results with a much smaller review.
I would really like to make the explicit models ergonomic enough that we can always just work in them.
But we are definitely not close to that
@Christian Reitwiessner has put a lot of effort into making Turing machines more ergonomic
And we are _closer_ than we were months or weeks ago
